extracted.intended_audience: students and researchers in sociology/psychology/communication studying humour
extracted.subtask_description: Identify and evaluate the social functions, types, and mechanisms of humour (especially ridicule and embarrassment), including developmental, conversational, cultural, and power-related aspects. Use these dimensions to analyze instances of humour and their effects on social order.

rubrics_metrics.name: Laughter as a rhetorical, learned device
rubrics_metrics.description: Laughter should be understood as rhetorical rather than a purely ‘natural’ reaction: it is a learned social device that can be mobilized in various ways.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat laughter as part of communicative technique: examine how it is taught, performed, and used to influence social interactions. Avoid explaining humour's universality solely in biological terms; instead investigate social practices that produce and shape laughter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ridicule as a necessary social function
rubrics_metrics.description: Ridicule may perform a necessary social function by discouraging infractions and helping to maintain social order generally (Bergson’s thesis: ridicule prevents social life from becoming rigid).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analyzing humour, consider whether mockery serves to enforce norms and sustain everyday codes of behaviour. Distinguish claims that ridicule is a harmful side-effect from arguments that it is constitutive of social regulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Embarrassment as the mechanism linking ridicule to conformity
rubrics_metrics.description: Embarrassment is a near-universal practice that protects everyday codes of behaviour: fear of ridicule/embarrassment encourages routine conformity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for instances where potential public embarrassment produces self-regulation. Consider how onlookers' laughter produces fear and how that fear functions to maintain social order across cultures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between disciplinary and rebellious humour
rubrics_metrics.description: Disciplinary humour mocks those who break social rules and aids rule maintenance; rebellious humour mocks the rules or rulers and can challenge authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classify humour by its social use and target: who is doing the mocking, who is being mocked, and to what end (enforcement vs challenge). Be aware this distinction rests on social position and use, not intrinsic joke properties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caution about classification and actor self-reports
rubrics_metrics.description: Classification of a particular humour instance as disciplinary or rebellious is often contentious because speakers justify their laughter and self-deceit can mask real motive or power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid relying solely on actors’ claims about intent; consider context, power relations, and likely effects. Expect claim-and-counterclaim dynamics and unverifiable mental states—classification may remain ambiguous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of parental ridicule in child socialization
rubrics_metrics.description: Parents’ laughter and mockery teach children both the rules of language/behaviour and how rule-breaking produces social responses (including how to mock others).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze early examples of laughter in child development to see how corrective mockery operates (inclusive vs exclusionary). Note the double-edged nature: it instructs politeness while also revealing and teaching rudeness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disciplinary laughter as gentle social instruction and initiation
rubrics_metrics.description: Laughter can function as a relatively mild form of discipline or initiation (e.g., in workplaces, apprenticeships, teams), instructing newcomers on norms while producing group solidarity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify humour that publicly marks deviations to educate or integrate members; distinguish inclusive corrective laughter from ridicule that wounds or excludes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Humour as flouting conversational maxims
rubrics_metrics.description: Much adult humour operates by flouting conversational maxims (relevance, order, clarity) — e.g., puns, irony — thereby creating comic effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analyzing jokes, map how they intentionally breach Gricean maxims or cooperative principles. Also assess whether the audience has the shared codes needed to recognize the breach as joking rather than as communicative failure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Joke-telling codes and signals
rubrics_metrics.description: Joke-telling has its own conversational codes (signals that mark a move from seriousness to joking); these codes must be followed for recipients to recognize material as a joke.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for explicit or implicit markers (tone, timing, prefaces) that indicate a joke. Absence of such markers can produce misunderstanding or genuine offence; analysts should check for those markers before attributing humorous intent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Taboo/forbidden content yields pleasure because of prohibition
rubrics_metrics.description: Humour about taboo or forbidden topics (dirty jokes, sick jokes, etc.) derives pleasure from the fact that such topics have been marked as forbidden.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine how prohibitions create the comic value of taboo material; note age/gender patterns (e.g., adolescents) and cultural variation in what counts as taboo.

rubrics_metrics.name: Power dynamics shape humour’s function and interpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: The social position of the laugher (superior, subordinate, outsider) and the target (powerful or powerless) shape whether humour functions repressively or contestingly; powerful actors can also present their humour as rebellious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess who benefits from the humour and how it reinforces or contests power. Beware of actors who claim a rebellious posture while exercising power; consider historical and institutional contexts (e.g., media co-option).

rubrics_metrics.name: Humour can unite and divide — social effects must be examined empirically
rubrics_metrics.description: Contrary to simple claims that ‘laughter only unites’, laughter can both unite groups and divide them by marking in-group norms and excluding others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investigate whether laughter enhances group solidarity or reinforces social boundaries (e.g., ethnic jokes marking ‘our’ accent as standard). Consider the social consequences rather than assuming unifying effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decommitment/face-saving function of humour
rubrics_metrics.description: Humour can be used post hoc to distance speakers from the serious meaning of an utterance (decommitment), serving as a face-saving device.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for attempts to recast an awkward or offensive comment as 'just a joke'; examine conversational evidence for whether the joke status was signalled originally. Recognize the impossibility of conclusively proving inner intent from recorded interaction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultural variability in norms and what is considered ludicrous
rubrics_metrics.description: Cultural differences determine what is judged ludicrous or unfunny; majority groups often treat their own norms as the implicit, unfunny standard against which others are mocked.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Account for cross-cultural differences in comedic targets and norms; be cautious of universalizing judgments about what is 'proper' or 'ludicrous'. Use ethnographic/contextual data to interpret jokes tied to accents, dress, or manners.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits on flouting: not all maxims can be broken simultaneously
rubrics_metrics.description: Although any conversational maxim can be broken to comic effect, breaking too many at once leads to meaninglessness rather than humour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze which specific maxims are breached and how the breach is constrained so recipients can still interpret the utterance as humorous. Recognize structural limits that keep humour interpretable.
